not_covered: While urban areas generally became wealthier in nominal terms, this prosperity was unevenly distributed, creating stark divides between high and low-income residents [Source: ev-2].

This shift concentrated high-income professionals in urban cores, driving a demographic realignment where nearly 80% of the country’s population growth for those under age 45 since 1980 was concentrated in metro areas with over 1 million residents [Source: ev-2] [Source: ev-1].
Gentrification accelerated sharply after 2000, affecting nearly 20% of lower-income neighborhoods in major cities compared to only 9% during the 1990s [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-2].

Despite this acceleration, gentrification remains geographically concentrated and rare nationally, with only 8% of all reviewed neighborhoods experiencing it since the year 2000 Census [Source: ev-1].
Other notable cities include Atlanta and Virginia Beach at 46.2%, Denver at 42.1%, and Austin at 39.7% [Source: ev-1].
In terms of raw volume, New York City had the highest number of gentrified tracts with 128, though its rate was lower at 29.8% due to a larger base of ineligible wealthy areas [Source: ev-1].
Conversely, cities like Detroit (2.8%), Las Vegas (2%), El Paso (0%), and Arlington, TX (0%) experienced little to no gentrification [Source: ev-1].
Atlanta and Miami followed closely at a Gini coefficient of 0.57 [Source: ev-2].
Affordability challenges have intensified due to diverging growth rates. [Source: ev-2]
This divergence is particularly acute on the West Coast, where California cities exhibit price-to-income ratios between 9.6 and 12.2, more than double the national average of 4.7 [Source: ev-2].
Gentrification has driven distinct demographic changes and displacement patterns [Source: ev-2].

Gentrifying neighborhoods recorded population increases and became whiter, with the share of non-Hispanic white residents increasing by an average of 4.3 percentage points [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-2].

In contrast, lower-income neighborhoods that did not gentrify experienced slight population losses of -2.4% and saw minority concentrations increase, resulting in a -5.0 percentage point change in white share [Source: ev-1].

Economic outcomes for residents diverged sharply based on neighborhood status; poverty rates dropped slightly by 0.7 percentage points in gentrifying tracts but climbed nearly 6.7 percentage points in eligible non-gentrifying low-income areas [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-2].
Additionally, educational gentrification is evident as urban areas now have 35% of residents with bachelor's degrees or higher, compared to 31% in suburbs and 19% in rural areas [Source: ev-2].

While specific neighborhoods became whiter during gentrification, the broader white population share fell by 7 points in urban cores and 8 points in suburbs since 2000 due to wider demographic shifts [Source: ev-2].
Despite this growth, gentrification remains geographically concentrated. [Source: ev-2]
